screens.title: Handling Multiple Exceptions and the finally Block
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn how Java helps you manage more than one kind of failure from the same block of code and how to guarantee cleanup after execution. We start by looking at multiple catch blocks: why their order matters and how the JVM picks the first matching handler. You'll see a concrete file-reading example that can throw an input-output error, a malformed-number error, or an unexpected runtime error. Next we'll explore multi-catch syntax introduced in Java 7, where several exception types can be handled by one block when the remedial action is identical. You'll also learn about polymorphic catches — catching a superclass to handle many related subclasses — and the tradeoffs this introduces for specific handling. Finally, we'll examine the finally block and why it always runs, even with returns or thrown exceptions, and then refactor the same example to use try-with-resources so resources close automatically. By the end you'll know when to use specific handlers, when to combine handlers, and why try-with-resources is the preferred pattern for AutoCloseable resources. Consider how these choices change how clearly your program reports errors and frees resources.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next screens you'll gain four concrete skills that make your Java programs safer and easier to maintain. First, you'll implement multiple catch blocks to respond to different exception types thrown by the same try block. Practically, that means distinguishing between a missing file and malformed data and reporting each clearly. Second, you'll learn how polymorphic catches let you handle a group of related exceptions by their shared superclass, which is useful when specific handling is not required but conflict with specificity must be avoided. Third, you'll apply finally blocks to guarantee critical cleanup runs, even when exceptions or returns occur, and you'll see common pitfalls like exceptions during close. Fourth, you'll adopt try-with-resources to automatically close AutoCloseable resources and reduce boilerplate. Each objective is paired with a small mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you know when you can confidently apply the pattern in your own code.

screens.title: Multiple catch blocks and handler ordering
screens.narratorSegment: When a try block throws an exception, the runtime looks for the first catch whose parameter type matches the thrown exception or is a superclass. This simple rule makes ordering vital: place specific exception types first, then broader types. For example, if a NumberFormatException and IOException could both occur in the same try block, and you place a generic Exception catch before them, the generic handler will always intercept the error and the specific handlers become unreachable. A common misconception is to think catch order only affects readability; in Java it affects correctness and may lead to compiler errors called "unreachable catch block". Concrete example: reading a line from a file and parsing it as an integer can throw either IOException or NumberFormatException. If you want distinct messages for each, write a catch for NumberFormatException first, then IOException, then a final catch(Exception) fallback. Key takeaway: order your catches from narrow to broad. Try a quick thought experiment: if you need identical handling for two unrelated exceptions, consider a multi-catch instead of duplicating code. That avoids ordering issues while keeping intent explicit.

keyIdea.title: Ordering rule
keyIdea.text: Catch blocks are checked top to bottom; put specific types before general types to ensure correct handlers run.

content.html:
Core Concept
Multiple catches and ordering
The JVM selects the first catch whose type matches the exception. Specific first, general last.
How it works
  • Thrown exception is matched against catch parameter types in order.
  • The first compatible catch executes; remaining catches are skipped.
  • Compiler enforces that more general catches cannot precede specific ones.
Common mistake
Placing catch (Exception e) before a specific catch makes the specific catch unreachable and hides useful distinctions.
Key Takeaway

Order catch blocks from most specific to most general to ensure intended handlers run and avoid unreachable-block errors.

Example: file read + parse
<!-- Escaped Java example -->
import java.io.BufferedReader;
import java.io.FileReader;
import java.io.IOException;

try {
  BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("data.txt"));
  String line = reader.readLine();
  int number = Integer.parseInt(line);
  System.out.println("Read number: " + number);
} catch (NumberFormatException e) {
  System.err.println("Invalid number format in file.");
} catch (IOException e) {
  System.err.println("I/O error while reading file.");
} catch (Exception e) {
  System.err.println("Unexpected error: " + e.getMessage());
}
Misconception
Putting Exception first only hides specific causes; it does not make the program safer.
Try this
Swap the catch order and compile; observe the compiler error for unreachable catch block.

screens.title: Specific catch blocks vs polymorphic catches
screens.narratorSegment: Catching by a superclass type is called polymorphic catching. It is convenient when several related exceptions require the same handling, but it trades off specificity. For example, catching IOException will also catch FileNotFoundException because it is a subclass. If you need different responses — say, a retry for a transient network IOException versus a configuration error for missing file — then separate catches are better. A misconception is thinking polymorphic catch automatically documents intent. It can obscure root causes if you rely solely on the superclass. On the other hand, too many specific catches can duplicate identical error handling. Use multi-catch when unrelated exceptions share handling, and use a superclass catch when the entire family truly needs the same recovery. Concrete scenario: when a file is absent you may offer a default configuration; when data is malformed you should prompt corrective action. Ask yourself: will future maintainers need different handling? If yes, prefer specific catches; otherwise polymorphism may simplify the code. Specific catch blocks vs polymorphic catches means polymorphic catches simplify code for uniform handling but reduce the ability to respond differently to distinct subclass failures.. In practical terms, when to handle subclasses separately or catch a shared superclass. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison
Specific vs Polymorphic Catches
Decide whether each exception type needs its own response or if a shared handler suffices.
Specific catches
Separate handling per exception type; clearer diagnostics and tailored recovery steps.
Polymorphic catch
Catch a superclass to handle a family of exceptions with identical remediation; less boilerplate but coarser control.
Key Takeaway

Match the handler granularity to the needed response: precise when behavior differs, polymorphic when uniform handling is sufficient.

Scenario breakdown
Missing file (FileNotFoundException)
Action: inform user or use a default file; may be recoverable by supplying path.
Malformed data (NumberFormatException)
Action: prompt repair of data or fallback value; distinct from I/O failures.
When to group
If both missing file and unreadable content should produce the same fallback, multi-catch or a superclass catch can reduce duplication.

screens.title: Multiple specific catch blocks — file read example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete example that reads a single line from a file and parses it as an integer, using multiple specific catch blocks to handle distinct failures. The try block opens a BufferedReader, reads a line, and calls integer parsing. If parsing fails, NumberFormatException runs and prints an explanatory error. If the file cannot be opened or read, IOException runs with a different message. Finally, a broad Exception catch handles any other unforeseen issues. A common misconception is that resources declared outside of try are always safe to close in finally without additional checks; in this pattern you must check for null before close because the constructor might have failed. Also note that close itself can throw an IOException; the sample wraps close inside its own try-catch within finally to avoid losing the original error. Example shows explicit close in finally; later we'll refactor to try-with-resources to avoid this ceremony. Try reading a missing file, a file with the text "42", and a file that contains "hello" to see which catch executes and whether the reader is closed.

keyIdea.title: Concrete example
keyIdea.text: Use multiple catches to report different problems clearly, and guard resource close calls inside finally.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Reading an integer with specific catches
<!-- Escaped Java example from chapter -->
import java.io.BufferedReader;
import java.io.FileReader;
import java.io.IOException;

public class MultipleCatchBlocks {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String fileName = "data.txt";
        BufferedReader reader = null;

        try {
            reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(fileName));
            String line = reader.readLine();
            int number = Integer.parseInt(line);
            System.out.println("Read number: " + number);
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            System.err.println("Error: The file contains invalid number format.");
            e.printStackTrace();
        } catch (IOException e) {
            System.err.println("Error: Could not read from file " + fileName);
            e.printStackTrace();
        } catch (Exception e) {
            System.err.println("An unexpected error occurred: " + e.getMessage());
            e.printStackTrace();
        } finally {
            System.out.println("Attempting to close the reader...");
            if (reader != null) {
                try {
                    reader.close();
                    System.out.println("Reader closed successfully.");
                } catch (IOException e) {
                    System.err.println("Error closing the reader: " + e.getMessage());
                    e.printStackTrace();
                }
            }
        }
        System.out.println("Program finished execution.");
    }
}
Explainer
  • NumberFormatException handles parsing errors when the text isn't numeric.
  • IOException handles file access problems like missing files or permission issues.
  • Exception acts as a last-resort fallback for other unexpected issues.
Misconception
Assuming finally that closes without its own try-catch can mask a second exception and hide the original failure.
Key Takeaway

Explicitly guard resource closures and prefer try-with-resources when possible to avoid nested cleanup code.

screens.title: Multi-catch with the vertical bar
screens.narratorSegment: Java 7 introduced multi-catch, which lets you handle several distinct exception types with a single catch block using the vertical bar separator. Use this when the recovery or reporting is identical for each type. For instance, if both NumberFormatException and IOException should produce the same diagnostic message and stack trace handling, you can write catch (NumberFormatException | IOException e). Two important details: first, the exception parameter is effectively final in a multi-catch, so you cannot reassign it. Second, the compile-time type is the nearest common superclass, meaning you can only call methods available on all listed types, such as getMessage and printStackTrace. A common misconception is to try to perform type-specific logic inside a multi-catch; if you need distinct logic, prefer separate catch blocks. Process summary: list exception types you want grouped, ensure their common behavior is truly the same, and remember that multi-catch improves readability by reducing duplicated code. After this, you'll see how try-with-resources further simplifies resource management. Multi-catch with the vertical bar means use multi-catch to consolidate identical handling for several exception types while respecting the effective finality of the exception variable.. In practical terms, combine handlers for identical recovery paths using the | operator. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Process Flow
Create a multi-catch for identical handling
Steps to decide and implement a multi-catch.
1. Identify identical responses
Check that exceptions will be handled the same way.
2. List types with |
Write catch (TypeA | TypeB e) and use common methods only.
3. Avoid type-specific logic
If you need per-type branches, revert to separate catch blocks.
<!-- Multi-catch example -->
try (BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("data.txt"))) {
  String line = reader.readLine();
  int number = Integer.parseInt(line);
  System.out.println(number);
} catch (NumberFormatException | IOException e) {
  System.err.println("Error related to reading or parsing: " + e.getMessage());
  e.printStackTrace();
}
Notes
  • The exception variable is implicitly final.
  • You can only call methods common to all listed types.
  • Multi-catch reduces duplication when handling is identical.
Key Takeaway

Group unrelated exceptions with multi-catch only when the remediation is identical; otherwise use specific catches.

screens.title: The finally block: guaranteed execution
screens.narratorSegment: The finally block is a guaranteed execution path that runs after try and its catch blocks, whether an exception was thrown, caught, or a return was executed inside the try. That guarantee makes finally the natural place for cleanup tasks such as closing streams or releasing locks. A key detail is that finally executes even when a return statement appears in the try or catch. However, finally can also change control flow if it throws its own exception or performs a return; this is a common pitfall because an exception inside finally can suppress an earlier exception. To avoid losing the original failure, wrap cleanup calls inside their own try-catch within finally, or prefer try-with-resources when working with AutoCloseable. Concrete example: close the BufferedReader inside a nested try-catch in finally to catch and handle IOException from close, while preserving the original exception. Ask yourself: does my cleanup code need to be resilient to its own failures? If so, add explicit handling or move to try-with-resources. The finally block: guaranteed execution means finally always executes after try/catch, making it essential for cleanup—but guard against exceptions thrown inside finally itself.. In practical terms, why finally always runs and how to use it safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition
finally: guaranteed cleanup
Use finally when you must execute code regardless of exceptions or return statements.
Best practice
Wrap close calls in their own try-catch inside finally to avoid losing the original exception if close throws.
Misconception
Assuming finally never alters exception propagation. If finally throws or returns, it can change which exception is seen by callers.
Annotated example
<!-- finally with guarded close -->
BufferedReader reader = null;
try {
  reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(fileName));
  // read and parse
} catch (Exception e) {
  // handle
} finally {
  if (reader != null) {
    try {
      reader.close();
    } catch (IOException closeEx) {
      // handle close exception without suppressing original
    }
  }
}
Key Takeaway

Use finally for necessary cleanup, but protect cleanup code so it cannot hide the primary failure.

screens.title: Exceptions during resource closing
screens.narratorSegment: Closing a resource can throw its own exception, and that can interfere with reporting the original error. For example, if reading fails and throws IOException, and then reader. close also throws IOException inside finally, you may end up with the close exception overshadowing the original, more informative one. A misconception is believing finally always preserves the original exception; it does not if the finally block itself throws. The manual pattern is to wrap close in a separate try-catch inside finally so that the original exception remains visible. Java's try-with-resources addresses this problem by automatically closing resources and suppressing secondary exceptions: if an exception occurs in the try and another occurs during automatic close, the original exception is propagated while the closing exception is recorded as a suppressed exception you can inspect programmatically. Practically, prefer try-with-resources for AutoCloseable resources to avoid manual nesting and to keep the original failure primary while still capturing close-time errors for diagnostics. Exceptions during resource closing means automatic resource management in try-with-resources preserves the original exception and records closing failures as suppressed exceptions.. In practical terms, how close() exceptions can suppress or complicate error reporting. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comparison
Manual finally vs try-with-resources
Which approach preserves the original exception and why.
Manual finally
You must nest a try-catch inside finally to handle close exceptions or risk losing the primary error.
Try-with-resources
Automatically closes resources and preserves the original exception while recording close exceptions as suppressed.

Key Takeaway

Avoid hiding the original failure. Use try-with-resources to keep the primary exception visible and capture close-time errors as suppressed exceptions.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Refactor: try-with-resources
<!-- Try-with-resources example -->
public class TryWithResourcesExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String fileName = "data.txt";

        try (BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(fileName))) {
            String line = reader.readLine();
            int number = Integer.parseInt(line);
            System.out.println("Read number: " + number);
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            System.err.println("Error: The file contains invalid number format.");
            e.printStackTrace();
        } catch (IOException e) {
            System.err.println("Error: Could not read from file " + fileName);
            e.printStackTrace();
        }
        System.out.println("Program finished execution.");
    }
}
Why prefer this
  • No finally needed to close the reader.
  • Original exceptions stay primary; close-time problems are suppressed and retrievable.
  • Cleaner, less error-prone resource management.
Key Takeaway

Prefer try-with-resources for AutoCloseable resources to reduce boilerplate and preserve useful exception information.

Hands-on Activity
Implement ConfigFileProcessor
Follow these steps to complete and test the starter code provided in the chapter.
  1. Implement readConfigValue using try-with-resources and BufferedReader.
  2. Catch FileNotFoundException, NumberFormatException, then IOException in that order.
  3. Print descriptive messages and stack traces for each error case.
  4. In main, create files for valid, bad, empty, and test the non-existent file case.
  5. Observe outputs and confirm the reader closes automatically.
Pitfall to avoid
Catching Exception too early hides specific causes. Keep specific catches before a general fallback.
Starter code snippet
<!-- Starter: method skeleton -->
public static int readConfigValue(String filePath) {
  int configValue = -1;
  try (BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(filePath))) {
    String line = reader.readLine();
    if (line != null) {
      configValue = Integer.parseInt(line.trim());
    } else {
      System.err.println("Warning: Config file " + filePath + " is empty.");
    }
  } catch (FileNotFoundException e) {
    System.err.println("Error: Configuration file not found at " + filePath);
    e.printStackTrace();
  } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
    System.err.println("Error: Invalid number format in configuration file " + filePath);
    e.printStackTrace();
  } catch (IOException e) {
    System.err.println("Error: An I/O problem occurred while reading " + filePath);
    e.printStackTrace();
  }
  return configValue;
}
Key Takeaway

Test every failure mode and prefer try-with-resources to avoid manual cleanup errors while keeping handlers specific where needed.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › What to Remember
What to Remember
Three cleanup and safety rules to apply every time you use resources.
Finally executes always
Use finally for code that must run regardless of prior exceptions or returns, but guard its contents.

Wrap close calls in their own try-catch to prevent close-time exceptions from hiding the primary error.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how Java helps you manage more than one kind of failure from the same block of code and how to guarantee cleanup after execution. We start by looking at multiple catch blocks: why their order matters and how the JVM picks the first matching handler. You'll see a concrete file-reading example that can throw an input-output error, a malformed-number error, or an unexpected runtime error. Next we'll explore multi-catch syntax introduced in Java 7, where several exception types can be handled by one block when the remedial action is identical. You'll also learn about polymorphic catches — catching a superclass to handle many related subclasses — and the tradeoffs this introduces for specific handling. Finally, we'll examine the finally block and why it always runs, even with returns or thrown exceptions, and then refactor the same example to use try-with-resources so resources close automatically. By the end you'll know when to use specific handlers, when to combine handlers, and why try-with-resources is the preferred pattern for AutoCloseable resources. Consider how these choices change how clearly your program reports errors and frees resources.

Over the next screens you'll gain four concrete skills that make your Java programs safer and easier to maintain. First, you'll implement multiple catch blocks to respond to different exception types thrown by the same try block. Practically, that means distinguishing between a missing file and malformed data and reporting each clearly. Second, you'll learn how polymorphic catches let you handle a group of related exceptions by their shared superclass, which is useful when specific handling is not required but conflict with specificity must be avoided. Third, you'll apply finally blocks to guarantee critical cleanup runs, even when exceptions or returns occur, and you'll see common pitfalls like exceptions during close. Fourth, you'll adopt try-with-resources to automatically close AutoCloseable resources and reduce boilerplate. Each objective is paired with a small mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you know when you can confidently apply the pattern in your own code.

This second objectives screen turns each competency into a practical verification step so you can check that you know how to apply the pattern in real code. For multiple catch blocks, you will write a try that reads from a file and implement separate catch blocks for malformed data, input and output failures, and a fallback for any other unexpected exception. For polymorphic catches, you'll practice replacing several sibling catch blocks with a single superclass catch and reflect on when that reduces clarity. For finally, you'll add explicit cleanup with its own nested try-catch to handle exceptions thrown while closing, and observe how finally still executes after a return. For try-with-resources, you'll refactor the file reading code to declare the BufferedReader in the try header and confirm the reader is closed automatically even when parsing fails. Each card includes a mnemonic and a clear milestone so you can test behavior with valid, invalid, and missing files.

When a try block throws an exception, the runtime looks for the first catch whose parameter type matches the thrown exception or is a superclass. This simple rule makes ordering vital: place specific exception types first, then broader types. For example, if a NumberFormatException and IOException could both occur in the same try block, and you place a generic Exception catch before them, the generic handler will always intercept the error and the specific handlers become unreachable. A common misconception is to think catch order only affects readability; in Java it affects correctness and may lead to compiler errors called "unreachable catch block". Concrete example: reading a line from a file and parsing it as an integer can throw either IOException or NumberFormatException. If you want distinct messages for each, write a catch for NumberFormatException first, then IOException, then a final catch(Exception) fallback. Key takeaway: order your catches from narrow to broad. Try a quick thought experiment: if you need identical handling for two unrelated exceptions, consider a multi-catch instead of duplicating code. That avoids ordering issues while keeping intent explicit.

Catching by a superclass type is called polymorphic catching. It is convenient when several related exceptions require the same handling, but it trades off specificity. For example, catching IOException will also catch FileNotFoundException because it is a subclass. If you need different responses — say, a retry for a transient network IOException versus a configuration error for missing file — then separate catches are better. A misconception is thinking polymorphic catch automatically documents intent. It can obscure root causes if you rely solely on the superclass. On the other hand, too many specific catches can duplicate identical error handling. Use multi-catch when unrelated exceptions share handling, and use a superclass catch when the entire family truly needs the same recovery. Concrete scenario: when a file is absent you may offer a default configuration; when data is malformed you should prompt corrective action. Ask yourself: will future maintainers need different handling? If yes, prefer specific catches; otherwise polymorphism may simplify the code. If the file cannot be opened or read, IOException runs with a different message. Finally, a broad Exception catch handles any other unforeseen issues.
